nameStory: The Sandhill Crane gets its name from the sandy grasslands, or 'sandhills,' where these magnificent birds often gather during migration and feeding. The name specifically comes from places like Nebraska's Sandhills region, where hundreds of thousands of cranes stop along the Platte River during their epic journeys north and south.
description: Sandhill Cranes are large, elegant birds standing about 3-4 feet tall with impressive 6-foot wingspans. They have long, thin necks, sturdy legs, and distinctive red caps on their heads that look like they're wearing crimson berets. Their bodies are covered in gray feathers that often appear rusty or brown-stained from iron-rich mud they preen with. These are among the most ancient bird species on Earth, with fossil evidence showing cranes virtually unchanged for millions of years.

idTips.label: Distinctive call
idTips.description: Their loud, rattling bugle call carries for miles - a prehistoric-sounding 'kar-r-r-r-oo' that seems to echo from deep within their chest. Once you hear it, you'll recognize it instantly.

idTips.label: Red crown patch
idTips.description: Adults have a bright red, bare skin patch on top of their head that looks like smooth leather and contrasts sharply with their gray neck feathers.

idTips.label: Flight posture
idTips.description: In flight, they stretch their neck straight forward and legs straight back, creating a perfect line. Their broad wings beat slowly with deep, powerful strokes.

idTips.label: Size and stance
idTips.description: Much larger than herons, they stand tall and upright on long, dark legs. Their posture is confident and stately, like a feathered aristocrat surveying their domain.

idTips.label: Dancing behavior
idTips.description: They perform elaborate dances with bowing, jumping, and wing-flapping that looks like joyful celebration. You might see them tossing sticks or grass in the air during these displays.

habitat: In New England, look for Sandhill Cranes in large open wetlands, marshy meadows, and agricultural fields, especially during migration periods. They prefer areas with shallow water for roosting and nearby grain fields or grasslands for feeding. You're most likely to spot them in river valleys and coastal plain areas where wetlands meet farmland.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration time in March and April when flocks pass through heading north. Listen for their calls overhead and watch for V-formations in the sky. They may stop to rest and feed in suitable wetlands.
seasonality.summer: Small numbers may remain to breed in northern New England's larger wetland complexes. Look for pairs with their rust-colored young, called colts, following behind in single file.
seasonality.fall: Another migration peak in October and November as they head south. Flocks may be larger and more visible as they stop to feed and build energy reserves for their long journey.
seasonality.winter: Rare in New England as most migrate to southern states. Any winter sightings are noteworthy and should be reported to local birding organizations.

funFact: Sandhill Cranes are living dinosaurs - they're one of the oldest bird species on Earth, with fossils dating back 2.5 million years, meaning they walked alongside saber-toothed cats and early human ancestors virtually unchanged from how they look today.
confusionNotes: Most often confused with Great Blue Herons, but cranes fly with necks extended forward (herons fold their necks back in an S-curve) and have much different calls. Remember: 'Cranes are confident' - they hold their necks straight out, while herons hunch theirs back.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name suggesting sandy areas, Sandhill Cranes are equally at home in wetlands and agricultural areas. They're one of the great conservation success stories, having recovered from near extinction in the early 1900s to healthy populations today thanks to hunting restrictions and habitat protection.
compareHints: Sandhill Cranes are the only crane species regularly seen in New England. They're much larger and more upright than any heron species, with broader wings and completely different flight posture. Their social behavior and loud calls also set them apart from the more solitary, quieter herons that share similar wetland habitats.
